sources.entry: Benchmarking tips (LLVM) - The compiler project's recipe for a quiet Linux host, governor, boost, SMT siblings, ASLR, a cpuset and tmpfs.

summary.title: Benchmarking tips
summary.one_liner: Learn the LLVM project's checklist for reducing measurement noise when benchmarking on Linux, including governor, Turbo Boost, SMT, ASLR, cpuset shielding and tmpfs.
takeaways: Use a high-resolution timer such as perf under Linux and run benchmarks multiple times to spot noise.
Disable frequency scaling, Turbo Boost, and address space randomization, and set the CPU governor to performance.
Use cset to shield CPU cores for the benchmarked program, leaving at least 2 cores when using perf, and disable the SMT siblings of the cores used.
Put programs, inputs, and outputs on tmpfs and consider static linking (-DLLVM_BUILD_STATIC=ON) to reduce storage and dynamic loading variation.
Low noise does not rule out measurement bias; the page cites Mytkowicz et al. (ASPLOS 2009) on this.
summary.summary: This LLVM documentation page gives practical advice for reducing noise when benchmarking a patch, starting with general steps like using a high-resolution timer, repeated runs, disabling background services, and static linking. It then provides OS-specific sections, with Linux commands for disabling address space randomization, setting the performance CPU governor, isolating cores with cset shield, disabling SMT sibling threads, and running under perf stat -r 10. A Linux Intel section covers disabling Turbo Boost via intel_pstate. The page states that with these settings perf variations below 0.1% can be expected, and it notes that low noise alone does not prevent measurement bias.
